description: Learn web security fundamentals: CIA triad, Authentication vs Authorization, HTTPS/TLS, Same-Origin Policy (SOP), CORS, and Principle of Least Privilege.

slides.title: Introduction to Web Security
slides.content:
# Welcome to Web Application Security 🛡️

Web application security is the discipline of protecting websites, web APIs, and online services from malicious threats, unauthorized access, and data breaches.

## Why Web Security Matters
- 💰 **Financial Impact**: The average cost of a data breach exceeds **$4.45 million** globally.
- ⚖️ **Legal & Regulatory Penalties**: Non-compliance with GDPR, HIPAA, or CCPA leads to catastrophic fines.
- 🏢 **Reputation & Trust**: 60% of small businesses close within 6 months of a major cyberattack.
- 🌐 **Pervasive Attack Surface**: Every line of frontend or backend code exposed to the internet is a potential target.

> 💡 **Core Mindset:** Security is not a feature you add at the end of development — it is an architectural mindset integrated into every stage of the software lifecycle.

slides.title: The CIA Triad
slides.content:
# The Cornerstone: The CIA Triad 🏛️

The **CIA Triad** is the foundational model guiding all information security policies.

## 1. Confidentiality (Privacy & Secrecy)
Ensures information is accessible only to those authorized to have access.

- *Controls*: Encryption (TLS/AES), strong access controls, masking sensitive data (credit cards).
- *Violation Example*: An attacker sniffing network packets to read passwords in plain text.

## 2. Integrity (Accuracy & Trustworthiness)
Guarantees that data has not been altered or tampered with by unauthorized parties.

- *Controls*: Digital signatures, cryptographic hashes (HMAC, SHA-256), database constraints.
- *Violation Example*: An attacker tampering with an HTTP POST request to change an item price from $500 to $1.

## 3. Availability (Uptime & Accessibility)
Ensures systems and services remain operational and accessible when needed by legitimate users.

- *Controls*: DDoS mitigation, auto-scaling, redundant backups, failovers.
- *Violation Example*: A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack flooding web servers.

slides.title: Authentication vs Authorization
slides.content:
# Authentication vs Authorization 🔑

These two security concepts are frequently confused, but serve completely different purposes.

## Comparison Matrix

| Aspect | Authentication (AuthN) | Authorization (AuthZ) |
|---|---|---|
| **Question Answered** | *"Who are you?"* | *"What are you allowed to do?"* |
| **Verification** | Identity verification | Permissions & access rights |
| **Timing** | First step (at login) | Every subsequent request |
| **Examples** | Password, Biometrics, 2FA/MFA, SMS OTP | Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), Admin rights |
| **HTTP Status Code** | `401 Unauthorized` (actually means unauthenticated!) | `403 Forbidden` |

```http_not
// 401: We don't know who you are. Please log in!
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized

// 403: We know who you are, but you are not allowed in this area!
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
```

slides.title: HTTPS and TLS Encryption
slides.content:
# HTTPS & Transport Layer Security (TLS) 🔒

**HTTPS** (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts communication between the client's browser and the web server using **TLS**.

## How Plain HTTP Exposes You

Under plain `http://`, all headers, cookies, passwords, and form data are transmitted in **plaintext** over public Wi-Fi and ISP routing nodes, allowing Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) packet sniffing.

## The TLS Handshake (Simplified)

1. **Client Hello**: Browser sends supported TLS versions and cryptographic cipher suites.
2. **Server Hello & Certificate**: Server presents its SSL/TLS certificate signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA).
3. **Asymmetric Key Exchange**: Browser verifies certificate authenticity and uses asymmetric encryption (RSA / Elliptic Curve) to negotiate a shared secret key.
4. **Symmetric Encryption**: Both parties switch to fast symmetric encryption (AES-GCM or ChaCha20) for all session data.

slides.title: The Same-Origin Policy (SOP)
slides.content:
# The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) 🌐

The **Same-Origin Policy** is the most crucial security mechanism in web browsers. It restricts how a document or script loaded by one origin can interact with a resource from another origin.

## What Defines an Origin?

An origin is defined by the exact combination of three components:

$$\text{Origin} = \text{Scheme (Protocol)} + \text{Host (Domain)} + \text{Port}$$

## Comparing Against `https://example.com:443`

| Target URL | Same Origin? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `https://example.com/api/user` | ✅ YES | Same scheme, host, and port |
| `https://example.com:8080` | ❌ NO | Different port (`8080` vs `443`) |
| `http://example.com` | ❌ NO | Different scheme (`http` vs `https`) |
| `https://api.example.com` | ❌ NO | Different host (subdomain) |
| `https://v2.example.com` | ❌ NO | Different host |

slides.title: Why SOP is Essential for Protection
slides.content:
# Why the Web Would Collapse Without SOP 🛡️

Imagine you are logged into your online bank (`mybank.com`), and an active authentication cookie is stored in your browser.

Now you visit an evil website: `malicious-site.com`.

## Without the Same-Origin Policy:
- A script running on `malicious-site.com` could execute:
  ```javascript_not
  // WITHOUT SOP: Evil script could read your bank account data!
  fetch('https://mybank.com/api/account-balance')
    .then(res => res.json())
    .then(data => sendToAttacker(data));
  ```
- The browser would attach your `mybank.com` cookie, and the attacker would read your financial records!

## With the Same-Origin Policy:
The browser intercepts the response and blocks `malicious-site.com` from reading any data returned by `mybank.com`!

slides.title: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
slides.content:
# Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) 🤝

While SOP protects users, modern applications legitimately need cross-origin requests (e.g. `frontend.app` calling `api.backend.com`).

**CORS** is an HTTP-header-based mechanism that allows a server to explicitly whitelist which origins can access its data.

## Server Response Headers for CORS

```http_not
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://frontend.app
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
```

> ⚠️ **Critical Misconception:** CORS is **NOT a security barrier for attackers**. Attackers can use cURL or Python scripts to bypass CORS entirely. CORS is a browser-enforced relaxation of the Same-Origin Policy!

slides.title: Preflight Requests: OPTIONS
slides.content:
# CORS Preflight Requests (`OPTIONS`) ✈️

For requests that could alter server state (like `PUT`, `DELETE`, or requests with custom headers like `Authorization`), the browser sends a **Preflight `OPTIONS` request** first.

```http_not
// 1. Browser asks permission before sending the real PUT request:
OPTIONS /api/user/101 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.backend.com
Origin: https://frontend.app
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization

// 2. Server gives approval:
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://frontend.app
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: PUT
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Authorization
Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400
```

Only after the preflight is approved does the browser transmit the actual `PUT` request!

slides.title: Principle of Least Privilege
slides.content:
# Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) 🛡️

The **Principle of Least Privilege** dictates that every user, program, and process must be granted only the minimum access rights necessary to perform its legitimate function.

## Real-World Engineering Applications

1. **Database Connections**: A public web app should connect to PostgreSQL using a role with `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE` on specific tables. It should **never** connect as the `postgres` superuser!
2. **API Keys**: Create separate read-only API keys for analytics reporting services instead of sharing administrative master tokens.
3. **Microservices & Containers**: Docker containers should run as non-root users (`USER node` instead of `root`).
4. **File Permissions**: Web upload folders should never have executable permissions (`chmod 777` is a critical vulnerability).

slides.title: Defense in Depth
slides.content:
# Defense in Depth (Layered Security) 🧅

**Defense in Depth** is the strategy of implementing multiple redundant layers of security defense throughout an application stack.

If an attacker breaches one defensive layer, subsequent layers prevent catastrophic exploitation.

```
Layer 1: Network & CDN        ➔ Cloudflare (DDoS mitigation, WAF, Bot detection)
Layer 2: Transport Layer      ➔ HTTPS / HSTS (Encryption in transit)
Layer 3: Browser Headers      ➔ Content Security Policy (CSP), X-Frame-Options
Layer 4: Application Logic   ➔ Input validation, Rate limiting, CSRF tokens
Layer 5: Authentication       ➔ Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), Argon2 hashing
Layer 6: Data Persistence     ➔ Parameterized queries, AES-256 database encryption
```

> 💡 **Key Insight:** Never rely on frontend validation alone. Never assume the network is private.

slides.title: The OWASP Top 10
slides.content:
# The OWASP Top 10 Standard 🏆

The **Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP)** is a non-profit foundation providing unbiased industry consensus on critical web security risks.

## Current OWASP Top 10 Categories

1. **A01: Broken Access Control** (Failures allowing users to access unauthorized data)
2. **A02: Cryptographic Failures** (Weak ciphers, sensitive data in plaintext)
3. **A03: Injection** (SQLi, Command Injection, XSS)
4. **A04: Insecure Design** (Architectural flaws and missing threat modeling)
5. **A05: Security Misconfiguration** (Default credentials, debug mode in production)
6. **A06: Vulnerable and Outdated Components** (Unpatched npm/pip packages)
7. **A07: Identification and Authentication Failures** (Credential stuffing, weak sessions)
8. **A08: Software and Data Integrity Failures** (Untrusted CI/CD pipelines)
9. **A09: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures** (Silent breaches)
10. **A10: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)**

slides.title: Threat Modeling Basics
slides.content:
# Threat Modeling & Risk Assessment 🎯

Threat modeling is the systematic process of identifying potential security threats before code is written.

## The STRIDE Model

Developed by Microsoft, STRIDE categorizes six common threat vectors:

- **S**poofing: Impersonating another user or system.
- **T**ampering: Modifying data or code in transit or at rest.
- **R**epudiation: Inability to prove an action was taken (lack of audit logs).
- **I**nformation Disclosure: Exposing confidential data to unauthorized parties.
- **D**enial of Service: Exhausting system memory or CPU to make services unavailable.
- **E**levation of Privilege: Gaining unauthorized administrative permissions.

slides.title: Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC)
slides.content:
# The Secure Software Development Lifecycle 🔄

Modern engineering practices "shift security left" by testing security in every phase of development:

1. **Requirements**: Define compliance goals (GDPR, PCI-DSS) and threat models.
2. **Design**: Establish architecture patterns (OAuth 2.0, zero-trust network boundaries).
3. **Coding**: Enforce static code analysis (SAST) and pre-commit security linters.
4. **Testing**: Dynamic application testing (DAST), automated penetration testing, dependency scanning (`npm audit`, Snyk).
5. **Deployment & Operations**: Continuous monitoring, log aggregation, bug bounty programs.

slides.title: Zero-Trust Architecture
slides.content:
# The Zero-Trust Security Paradigm 🔒

Traditional security relied on the "perimeter model" (like a medieval castle with a moat): anything inside the corporate VPN was trusted.

**Zero-Trust** operates on the principle:

> *"Never Trust, Always Verify."*

## The 3 Tenets of Zero Trust

1. **Verify Explicitly**: Always authenticate and authorize based on all available data points (user identity, location, device health, service).
2. **Use Least Privilege Access**: Limit user access with Just-In-Time (JIT) and Just-Enough-Access (JEA).
3. **Assume Breach**: Minimize blast radius by segmenting networks, encrypting all internal communications, and actively hunting for threats.

slides.title: Real-World Architecture: Multi-Layer Perimeter
slides.content:
# Real-World Example: Architecture of a Secure Web Service 🏛️

```http_not
Client Browser
     │  (1) TLS 1.3 Encryption / HTTPS Only (HSTS)
     ▼
Edge CDN / Cloudflare
     │  (2) DDoS Mitigation, WAF, Bot Blocking, Strict CORS
     ▼
Reverse Proxy / Nginx
     │  (3) Rate Limiting, Security Headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options)
     ▼
API Service (Node.js / Express)
     │  (4) JWT Signature Validation, Input Validation, Principle of Least Privilege
     ▼
PostgreSQL Database
        (5) Parameterized SQL, Encrypted at Rest (AES-256), Dedicated Non-Superuser Role
```

slides.title: Common Fundamental Security Mistakes
slides.content:
# Top Security Misconceptions & Mistakes ⚠️

1. **"CORS protects my API from hackers"**: False! CORS only instructs compliant browsers not to share responses. Attackers can call your API directly using Python or cURL.
2. **"Security through Obscurity"**: Renaming `/admin` to `/secret-door-123` is useless against automated scanners.
3. **Trusting Client-Side Validation**: Never rely on HTML5 `required` or JavaScript regex alone. Attackers can bypass browser code effortlessly.
4. **Hardcoding Secrets**: Storing API keys or database passwords in Git repositories is the #1 cause of cloud breaches.

slides.title: Summary: Security Fundamentals
slides.content:
# Security Fundamentals: Summary 📋

## Key Takeaways
- **CIA Triad**: Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability form the pillars of security.
- **AuthN vs AuthZ**: Authentication verifies identity; Authorization verifies permissions.
- **HTTPS/TLS**: Encrypts traffic in transit; protects against eavesdropping and tampering.
- **Same-Origin Policy (SOP)**: Isolates web origins based on protocol, domain, and port.
- **CORS**: A browser-side relaxation of SOP; not an API security shield.
- **Least Privilege**: Grant minimal necessary permissions to users, services, and databases.

slides.title: Next Steps: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
slides.content:
# Ahead: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) ⚔️🛡️

Now let's examine one of the most destructive and common web vulnerabilities.

## Topics Ahead:
- **Stored XSS (Persistent)**: Attacks saved directly into databases
- **Reflected XSS (Non-Persistent)**: Attacks reflected in query parameters
- **DOM-based XSS**: Client-side execution vulnerabilities
- **Defenses**: Context-aware output encoding, DOMPurify sanitization, and input validation

Let's master XSS defense! 🚀
